steps.body: Draw one card from twenty cards numbered 1–20. The twenty outcomes are the **sample space**. An **event** is just a subset of it: "multiple of 3" is the set {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}. Because every card is equally likely, a probability is a count: P(A) = (outcomes in A) ÷ 20.
Each cell is one card. Shade the event.

widget.prompt: The 20 cells are the 20 cards. Shade every card that is a multiple of 3, so the shaded fraction equals P(multiple of 3) = 3/10.
widget.successFeedback: Six cells — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Six out of twenty is 3/10, exactly the fraction you shaded.
widget.lowFeedback: Not enough cells yet. Count the multiples of 3 up to 20: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 — that is six cards, and 6/20 = 3/10.
widget.highFeedback: Too many shaded. 21 would be the seventh multiple of 3, but the deck stops at 20 — only six cards qualify.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 3/10 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 5/10 here — and 3 is less. Swap in 7/10 and the same test says more: halve the denominator, compare, and the check never changes. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

steps.body: A = multiple of 3. B = greater than 15.
explanationVariants: A ∩ B needs **both** conditions at once. Only 18 is a multiple of 3 *and* above 15, so A ∩ B = {18}.
Overlay the two lists: A = {3,6,9,12,15,18} and B = {16,17,18,19,20}. The only number on both lists is 18.

widget.prompt: Which set is A ∩ B (the outcomes in A **and** B)?

options.feedback: Exactly — 18 is the only card that is both a multiple of 3 and greater than 15.
That is A ∪ B — every card in either event. Intersection keeps only the cards that satisfy both conditions at once.
Those are the cards in B that are *not* in A. The intersection is what the two events share, not what separates them.

options.label: { } (no outcomes)
options.feedback: Empty would mean the events cannot co-occur, but 18 satisfies both — it is a multiple of 3 and it is above 15.

explanationVariants: A has 6 cards, B has 5, and they share 18. Adding 6 + 5 counts 18 twice, so subtract it once: 6 + 5 − 1 = 10.
List A ∪ B outright: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 — ten distinct cards.

widget.prompt: How many cards are in A ∪ B (multiple of 3 **or** greater than 15)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 + 5. Card 18 lives in both events, so a plain sum counts it twice — subtract the shared card once to get 10.
That is the size of A ∩ B. The union is everything in either event, not only what they share.
That is only A. The union also collects 16, 17, 19 and 20 from B.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count each card once: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 — ten cards. Adding 6 + 5 double-counts 18.

steps.body: Picture the two events as overlapping circles. The middle holds outcomes in **both**; the outer petals hold outcomes in only one; everything outside is in **neither**. That picture is why counting a union means adding the two circles and then removing the middle once — it was counted twice.

explanationVariants: A = multiples of 3, B = above 15. A card is in the middle only if it clears both tests; 18 is the only one.
Test each card twice — once against "multiple of 3", once against "greater than 15" — and its two answers place it.

widget.prompt: Sort each card by where it sits for A = multiple of 3 and B = greater than 15.

buckets.label: In A ∪ B, but not both

items.feedback: 18 passes both tests: it is 3 × 6, and it is above 15. That is the intersection.
9 is a multiple of 3 but not above 15, so it is in the union through A alone.
17 is above 15 but not a multiple of 3, so it joins the union through B alone.
20 is above 15 but 20 ÷ 3 is not whole, so it is in B only.
7 fails both tests — not a multiple of 3, not above 15 — so it sits outside both circles.
4 is not a multiple of 3 and it is well below 15, so it belongs to neither event.

widget.missFeedback: Check each card against both conditions separately, then place it where its two answers say.
widget.successFeedback: All six placed correctly — you read the Venn picture straight off the two conditions.

hints: C = even and D = multiple of 5 both live in the 1–20 deck. How big is each?
C has 10 cards and D has 4 (5, 10, 15, 20). Which cards are in both?
10 and 20 are in both, so |C ∪ D| = 10 + 4 − 2.
explanationVariants: Count the union directly: all ten evens, plus 5 and 15 from D (10 and 20 are already counted) → 12 cards.

widget.prompt: C = even card, D = multiple of 5. How many of the 20 cards are in C ∪ D?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 10 + 4 with no correction. Cards 10 and 20 are even *and* multiples of 5, so they were counted twice.
That is |C ∩ D| — just 10 and 20. The union is far bigger: every even card plus 5 and 15.
That is C alone. The union also picks up the odd multiples of 5, namely 5 and 15.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add and correct: 10 evens + 4 multiples of 5 − 2 shared (10 and 20) = 12 cards.

steps.body: Events are sets, and probability is counting.
takeaways: An event is a subset of the sample space; with equally likely outcomes, P(event) = count ÷ total.
A ∩ B = both at once; A ∪ B = at least one.
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| — the overlap is counted twice unless you remove it.
steps.teaser: Next: the fastest probability trick there is — count what you *don't* want, and subtract.

concept.body: Two words do all the work. **And** (∩) keeps an outcome only if it passes **both** tests. **Or** (∪) keeps it if it passes **at least one**. So the intersection is always the smaller set — it lives inside the union.

explanationVariants: Every outcome that passes both tests certainly passes at least one, so A ∩ B always sits inside A ∪ B.
Intersection is the strict club (two conditions); union is the open door (one condition is enough).

widget.prompt: For any two events, which statement is always true?

options.label: A ∩ B can never be larger than A ∪ B
options.feedback: Right — passing both tests means passing at least one, so the intersection is contained in the union.

options.label: A ∩ B is always larger than A ∪ B
options.feedback: That reverses it. Requiring two conditions can only shrink a set; requiring just one can only grow it.

options.label: A ∩ B and A ∪ B always have the same size
options.feedback: They match only when A and B are the same event. Any outcome in just one of them makes the union strictly bigger.
